title: How to Solve Apartment WiFi Dead Zones in 2026
summary: Learn how to fix WiFi dead zones in apartment buildings with network design strategies, access point placement, and managed WiFi solutions for reliable coverage.
body_text: Key Takeaways: How to Solve Apartment WiFi Dead Zones WiFi dead zones in apartments typically result from building materials, outdated infrastructure and poor access point placement rather than insufficient bandwidth. A professional site survey identifies signal weak spots and guides strategic access point deployment for consistent coverage across units and amenity areas. Managed WiFi solutions from providers such as Elauwit centralize network monitoring and support, eliminating dead zones while reducing property team workload. Retrofitting older buildings requires balancing infrastructure upgrades with minimal resident disruption during the cutover process. Property-wide network design with enterprise-grade access points delivers 200-300 basis points of NOI improvement by reducing complaints and boosting resident satisfaction. What Causes WiFi Dead Zones in Apartment Buildings? WiFi dead zones occur when wireless signals fail to reach certain areas of your property. In apartment buildings, these coverage gaps frustrate residents and generate support calls that consume your property team's time. Understanding the root causes helps you identify the right solution. Dead zones aren't random. They follow predictable patterns based on building characteristics and network design decisions made years ago. Building Materials That Block WiFi Signals Concrete walls, metal studs and plaster with wire lath absorb and reflect WiFi signals. A single concrete floor can reduce signal strength by 50% or more. Older buildings constructed before WiFi existed often have the densest materials. Elevator shafts and stairwells create vertical barriers. HVAC ductwork acts as an unintentional Faraday cage in many hallways. These structural elements don't change, so your network design must account for them. Outdated Network Infrastructure Many existing apartment buildings run on legacy coax or Cat5 cabling installed decades ago. This infrastructure can't deliver the symmetrical gigabit speeds modern residents expect. The wiring itself becomes a bottleneck before the signal ever reaches the access point. Single-router setups in each unit compound the problem. Consumer-grade routers weren't designed for the building density of multifamily environments, where dozens of networks compete on overlapping channels. Network Congestion and Interference A 200-unit building might have 200 individual routers broadcasting on the same handful of channels. This creates interference that degrades performance for everyone. The 2.4 GHz band becomes unusable during peak evening hours when residents stream, game and video call simultaneously. Device proliferation amplifies the challenge. The average resident now connects 5-9 devices to WiFi. Smart thermostats, doorbells, speakers and appliances compete with laptops and phones for bandwidth. How to Identify WiFi Dead Zones in Your Property Before fixing dead zones, you need to know exactly where they are. Guessing leads to wasted equipment and persistent complaints. A systematic approach saves money and delivers better outcomes. Conducting a Professional Site Survey A site survey maps signal strength throughout your building using specialized equipment. Technicians walk every floor, unit and amenity space while measuring actual WiFi performance. The result is a heat map showing exactly where coverage fails. Professional surveys also identify interference sources and recommend access point locations. This data-driven approach guarantees equipment goes where it's needed rather than where it's convenient to install. Analyzing Resident Complaint Patterns Your maintenance ticket system contains valuable data. Track which units and floors generate the most connectivity complaints. Look for clusters that indicate systemic issues rather than individual resident problems. Common complaint patterns reveal dead zone locations: "WiFi drops when I'm in the bedroom," "Can't get signal near the windows," or "Internet cuts out every evening." These specifics point to coverage gaps and congestion issues. Testing Signal Strength Across Units and Amenity Areas Walk your property with a WiFi analyzer app. Check signal strength in unit corners, bathrooms and balconies where residents commonly report problems. Test amenity spaces during peak usage times. Document your findings with photos and measurements. This baseline data helps you evaluate the effectiveness of any improvements you make. What Are the Best Solutions for Apartment WiFi Dead Zones? Solving dead zones requires matching the solution to your building's specific challenges. A 1960s garden-style community needs different approaches than a 2015 mid-rise. Here are the proven methods ranked by effectiveness. Property-Wide Managed WiFi Networks The most effective solution replaces the patchwork of individual resident routers with a single, professionally designed network. Enterprise-grade access points mounted throughout the building deliver consistent coverage from unit to unit and into amenity areas. Elauwit designs managed WiFi networks specifically for multifamily communities. With 38,000+ units under contract across 25 states, Elauwit's team understands how apartment buildings actually operate. Residents connect to their own private, secure network and roam throughout the property without drops. This approach eliminates interference from competing networks. One coordinated system manages channels, power levels and device loads automatically. Dead zones disappear because coverage is engineered rather than accidental. Strategic Access Point Placement Access point location determines coverage quality. Hallway-mounted units serve multiple apartments through walls. In-unit access points ensure strong signals in every room. The right choice depends on your building's construction and wiring. Key placement principles: Mount access points at ceiling height where fewer obstructions exist Position units away from metal objects and electrical panels Space access points based on wall density, not just square footage Plan for amenity areas such as pools and fitness centers separately Infrastructure Upgrades for Older Buildings Sometimes dead zones trace back to the physical network infrastructure. Replacing legacy coax with fiber or Cat6a cabling enables higher speeds and supports more access points per floor. Infrastructure upgrades require careful planning in occupied buildings. Elauwit's retrofit and network takeover approach includes cutover planning and resident communication support to minimize disruption during the transition. How Does Managed WiFi Eliminate Dead Zones? Managed WiFi differs fundamentally from bulk internet or traditional ISP service. Understanding the distinction helps you evaluate which approach fits your portfolio. Unified Network Architecture A managed WiFi provider deploys and controls all network equipment throughout your property. Access points work together as a coordinated system rather than competing islands. The network automatically balances loads and steers devices to optimal bands. This unified approach enables features impossible with individual routers: band steering to push devices to less congested frequencies, automatic channel selection to avoid interference and centralized security updates across all equipment. Centralized Monitoring and Support With managed WiFi, the provider monitors network health 24/7 and responds to issues before residents notice. When problems arise, support staff troubleshoot remotely and can resolve many issues without dispatching technicians. Elauwit handles resident support directly. Real humans answer in less than 30 seconds. Property teams stop fielding internet complaints and focus on higher-value work. This accountability model means one partner owns the entire experience from design through ongoing operations. Consistent Coverage Across All Areas Managed networks are designed for complete coverage from the start. Site surveys identify every potential dead zone. Access points are placed to eliminate gaps rather than added reactively after complaints. Residents experience the same reliable connection whether they're in their unit, the clubhouse or walking to the mailroom. Devices hand off between access points without dropping. The "follow-me" network experience keeps residents connected wherever they go on your property. What Should Property Owners Consider Before Upgrading WiFi? A WiFi upgrade is an infrastructure investment. The financial and operational implications deserve careful evaluation before committing. Ownership vs. Service Models Two primary commercial structures exist for managed WiFi. Owner-funded (Managed Services): You invest in the network infrastructure and own the equipment. Higher upfront cost, but you capture more value over time and retain full control. Provider-funded (Network-as-a-Service): The provider owns the infrastructure and delivers connectivity as a monthly service with no upfront capital. Elauwit offers Network-as-a-Service with $0 upfront cost, making enterprise-grade WiFi accessible for properties that need to preserve capital. Pick the model that fits your asset strategy. Both structures deliver the same network quality and resident experience. Financial Impact on NOI Properties with managed connectivity typically see 200-300 basis points of NOI improvement. The lift comes from multiple sources: reduced turnover costs as resident satisfaction increases, lower operational burden on property teams and potential revenue from connectivity fees. At a 5.5% cap rate, that NOI improvement translates directly to asset value. A 300-unit community capturing $70 per unit monthly adds meaningful value to your portfolio. Deployment Timeline and Resident Impact New construction projects can have connectivity designed in from day one. Retrofits require more coordination. Expect 4-6 months for a typical deployment, including assessment, design, installation and cutover. The key question for occupied properties: how will you minimize disruption during installation? A good provider handles resident communication and schedules work to avoid peak hours. The goal is getting residents online on the new network with as little friction as possible. How Do You Prevent Future WiFi Dead Zones? Solving today's dead zones is only half the challenge. Building a network that stays reliable as technology evolves protects your investment. Designing for Future Device Loads Resident device counts will keep growing. Smart home technology, work-from-home setups and streaming habits all trend upward. Your network should have headroom for these increases. WiFi 6 and WiFi 6E access points support more simultaneous devices with lower latency. A 10-gig fiber backbone throughout the property ensures you can upgrade wireless equipment without replacing cabling. Ongoing Network Monitoring and Optimization Networks degrade over time without maintenance. Firmware updates, equipment replacement and configuration adjustments keep performance consistent. Managed providers handle this work continuously. Monitoring also catches emerging dead zones before they generate complaints. As buildings settle and furniture gets rearranged, coverage patterns shift. Proactive optimization addresses these changes. Choosing a Provider with Long-Term Accountability Your network will outlast multiple lease cycles. The provider you choose today will be your partner for years. Look for stability, track record and clear accountability. Elauwit is the only publicly traded managed service provider dedicated exclusively to residential communities (Nasdaq: ELWT). That public-company accountability means audited financials, disclosed performance and long-term stability you can count on. Eliminating Apartment WiFi Dead Zones Requires a Strategic Approach WiFi dead zones in apartment buildings result from predictable causes: building materials, infrastructure limitations and network design decisions. Solving them requires understanding your specific property's challenges and selecting the right combination of infrastructure upgrades and managed services. Property-wide managed WiFi delivers the most complete solution. A coordinated network eliminates interference, professional design ensures coverage, and centralized support removes the burden from your property team. The financial case is compelling: improved NOI, reduced turnover and enhanced asset value. If your residents are complaining about dead zones, the problem won't fix itself. Contact Elauwit to schedule a network assessment and learn how managed WiFi can eliminate connectivity gaps across your portfolio. FAQs about How to Solve Apartment WiFi Dead Zones What is the main cause of WiFi dead zones in apartments? Building materials such as concrete, metal studs and plaster absorb and reflect WiFi signals, creating coverage gaps. When combined with legacy wiring and interference from dozens of competing resident routers, dead zones become widespread in older multifamily properties. How much does it cost to fix WiFi dead zones in an apartment building? Costs vary based on building size, construction type and existing infrastructure. Elauwit offers Network-as-a-Service with no upfront capital, making managed WiFi accessible regardless of your capital budget. Contact us for a property-specific assessment. Can mesh WiFi systems fix dead zones in apartments? Consumer mesh systems help individual units but don't solve building-wide issues. Each resident's mesh network still competes with neighbors for channels. Property-wide managed WiFi coordinates all access points as a single system, eliminating interference between units. How long does it take to install managed WiFi in an apartment building? Elauwit typically completes deployments in 4-6 months, including site survey, network design, installation and cutover. New construction projects can align with build schedules for day-one resident readiness. Retrofits require additional coordination to minimize disruption. Will upgrading WiFi infrastructure disrupt current residents? A good provider plans the cutover carefully to minimize impact. Elauwit includes resident communication support and schedules work to avoid peak usage times. The goal is getting residents online on the new network quickly, typically within minutes of the switch. What is the difference between bulk internet and managed WiFi? Bulk internet delivers bandwidth to each unit, but residents still manage their own routers and experience. Managed WiFi adds property-wide infrastructure, professional network design and ongoing support. Residents get consistent coverage everywhere on the property with one accountable partner handling issues.

title: ¿Cómo recibir dinero del exterior en Bolivia?
summary: Conoce cómo cobrar servicios desde el exterior en Bolivia y compara transferencias, cuentas en dólares y plataformas de pago.
body_text: Conclusiones clave Una cuenta global permite recibir pagos internacionales directamente en USD. Los bancos bolivianos pueden recibir transferencias internacionales vía SWIFT. El SIN contempla una factura específica para exportaciones de servicios. Si trabajas de forma remota desde Bolivia para una empresa o cliente extranjero, puedes recibir tus pagos mediante una transferencia bancaria internacional, una plataforma de pagos o una cuenta global en dólares. La mejor opción depende de las comisiones, el método de pago del cliente y la posibilidad de mantener tus ingresos en USD. Para un trabajador remoto, freelancer o contractor boliviano, recibir dinero del exterior significa cobrar por servicios prestados a una empresa o cliente ubicado fuera de Bolivia. Las principales alternativas son: Transferencia bancaria internacional mediante SWIFT. Plataformas de pago utilizadas por empresas y clientes internacionales (Deel, Ontop, Stripe, etc.). Cuenta global en dólares con datos bancarios de Estados Unidos. Transferencias ACH o Wire cuando el pagador se encuentra en Estados Unidos. La elección depende principalmente de cómo puede pagar tu cliente, cuánto cuesta recibir el dinero y qué quieres hacer después con tus dólares . Transferencia bancaria internacional Una transferencia internacional permite que una empresa extranjera envíe el pago directamente a una cuenta bancaria en Bolivia. Para recibirla, normalmente tendrás que proporcionar al pagador información como: Nombre completo del beneficiario. Número de cuenta. Nombre y dirección del banco. Código SWIFT/BIC. Información adicional solicitada por la entidad bancaria. El principal punto a evaluar son los costos. Una transferencia internacional puede involucrar al banco emisor, al banco receptor y a bancos corresponsales. ASFI publica los tarifarios de las entidades financieras bolivianas para que los usuarios puedan comparar los costos de las operaciones con el exterior. En abril de 2026, ASFI actualizó el reglamento sobre tasas, comisiones y tarifas aplicables a los servicios financieros, incluyendo las operaciones relacionadas con transferencias y giros al exterior. Esta opción puede ser adecuada si tu empleador solo trabaja con transferencias bancarias internacionales o si necesitas recibir pagos directamente en una cuenta bancaria boliviana. Plataformas de pago para freelancers y trabajadores remotos Otra posibilidad es utilizar una plataforma de pagos que sea compatible con el país donde resides y con el método de pago de tu cliente. Antes de elegir una plataforma para cobrar como freelancer en Bolivia , comprueba cuatro aspectos: Si permite recibir pagos desde el país donde está tu cliente. Si acepta pagos de empresas o terceros. Cuánto cobra por recibir el dinero. Cómo puedes retirar posteriormente los fondos en Bolivia. No todas las plataformas que permiten enviar dinero internacionalmente permiten las mismas operaciones para quienes reciben fondos. Por eso, si tu objetivo es cobrar servicios profesionales desde Bolivia , no basta con comprobar que una plataforma "funciona en Bolivia": también debes verificar específicamente sus funciones de recepción y retiro. Cuenta global en dólares Una cuenta global puede ser especialmente útil para trabajadores remotos que cobran regularmente en dólares. Wallbit ofrece una cuenta en dólares de Estados Unidos con routing number y account number , que permite recibir pagos mediante transferencias ACH y Wire. Los depósitos ACH y Wire son gratuitos en todos los planes. Además, Wallbit permite recibir pagos de terceros cuando corresponden a actividades comerciales legítimas, incluyendo pagos de empresas a proveedores de servicios y cobros de profesionales independientes en USD. Esto permite que un cliente o empresa de Estados Unidos pueda pagar directamente a tus datos bancarios estadounidenses, sin tener que realizar necesariamente una transferencia internacional hacia un banco boliviano. Wallbit también ofrece depósitos en moneda local para usuarios de Bolivia y opciones para retirar fondos en moneda local. ACH vs. Wire: ¿cuál conviene para cobrar desde Estados Unidos? Las tarifas se aplican principalmente al momento de retirar fondos, según el método y el plan contratado. ¿Cuál es la mejor forma de cobrar en dólares desde Bolivia? Para un trabajador remoto, freelancer o contractor, la mejor alternativa depende del tipo de relación que tengas con el pagador. Si trabajas para una empresa extranjera Si recibes un salario o pago mensual y la empresa utiliza transferencias bancarias de Estados Unidos, una cuenta global en dólares puede simplificar el proceso. Por ejemplo, los usuarios de Wallbit en Bolivia pueden utilizar una cuenta en EE.UU. para recibir pagos de plataformas como Deel, Upwork y Stripe. Si eres freelancer y tienes varios clientes Si trabajas con diferentes clientes internacionales, una cuenta que permita recibir pagos de terceros puede ayudarte a centralizar tus ingresos. En este caso, compara especialmente: Comisión por recibir cada pago. Monedas disponibles. Métodos de transferencia aceptados. Posibilidad de mantener el saldo en USD. Costo de retirar a Bolivia. Límites de recepción y retiro. En Wallbit, los depósitos ACH y Wire no tienen comisión. Para retiros ACH, la tarifa publicada actualmente es de 1% con un mínimo de USD 5 en el plan Classic , mientras que los retiros Wire tienen una comisión de 1% con un mínimo de USD 25 . Los planes Pro y Max tienen tarifas de retiro inferiores. Si quieres mantener tus ingresos en dólares Este punto puede ser determinante. Si cobras USD pero el proveedor convierte automáticamente tu saldo a moneda local, pierdes la posibilidad de decidir cuándo realizar la conversión. Una cuenta global en USD permite recibir y conservar el dinero en dólares antes de retirarlo o utilizarlo. Además, el tipo de cambio utilizado para convertir los fondos puede tener un impacto significativo en el monto final que recibes en Bolivia. El BCB publica diariamente las cotizaciones oficiales. Por ejemplo, su tabla del 28 de julio de 2026 registró un tipo de cambio oficial de Bs 11,54 por USD. Por eso, al comparar métodos para cobrar desde el exterior, no debes mirar únicamente la comisión: también debes comprobar qué tipo de cambio se aplica cuando conviertes tus dólares a bolivianos . ¿Cómo facturar servicios a clientes extranjeros desde Bolivia? Cobrar desde el exterior no elimina las obligaciones fiscales asociadas a la prestación del servicio. El Servicio de Impuestos Nacionales (SIN) contempla específicamente la Factura Comercial de Exportación de Servicios para contribuyentes que exportan servicios. Este documento figura como una categoría habilitada dentro del sistema de facturación y es emitido sin derecho a crédito fiscal. El SIN también explica que existe exportación de servicios cuando una actividad desarrollada dentro de Bolivia proporciona una ventaja o beneficio a una persona situada en el exterior, que utiliza o aprovecha económicamente el resultado y paga una contraprestación. Por ejemplo, un desarrollador que trabaja desde Bolivia para una empresa estadounidense, un diseñador que presta servicios a una compañía extranjera o un consultor que trabaja para clientes internacionales pueden encontrarse dentro de este supuesto, dependiendo de las características concretas de la operación. La forma de cobrar —banco, plataforma de pagos o cuenta global— no determina por sí sola el tratamiento tributario de la actividad. ¿Qué debes comparar antes de elegir dónde cobrar? Conversión ¿Qué tipo de cambio utiliza? Retiro ¿Cuánto cuesta enviar el dinero a Bolivia? Método ¿Acepta ACH, Wire o SWIFT? Pagador ¿Puede tu cliente utilizar ese método? Moneda ¿Puedes conservar el saldo en USD? Límites ¿Existe un límite mensual o por operación? Documentación ¿Qué comprobantes o datos pueden solicitarte? ASFI publica los tarifarios de las entidades financieras bolivianas precisamente para facilitar la comparación de productos y servicios financieros. Para un profesional que recibe pagos todos los meses, esta comparación es más relevante que elegir simplemente la plataforma con la comisión nominal más baja. Conclusión Para un trabajador remoto, freelancer o contractor que trabaja desde Bolivia para clientes internacionales , recibir dinero del exterior no se reduce a encontrar una plataforma que acepte pagos internacionales. Hay que comparar el método de recepción, las comisiones, el tipo de cambio, la posibilidad de mantener los fondos en USD y el costo de retirarlos en Bolivia. Las transferencias SWIFT siguen siendo una alternativa cuando el cliente paga directamente a bancos bolivianos. Para quienes cobran regularmente desde Estados Unidos, una cuenta global en dólares con ACH y Wire puede ofrecer un proceso más directo. Wallbit permite a usuarios de Bolivia recibir pagos en USD mediante ACH y Wire sin comisión de depósito , mantener sus fondos en dólares y posteriormente retirarlos en moneda local. title: Lithium Argentina Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results
summary: ZUG, Switzerland, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lithium Argentina AG (“ Lithium Argentina ” or the “ Company ”) ( TSX: LAR) ( NYSE: LAR) today announced its second quarter 2026 results. Unless otherwise stated, results are presented in United States dollars on a 100% basis.
body_text: ZUG, Switzerland, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lithium Argentina AG (“ Lithium Argentina ” or the “ Company ”) ( TSX: LAR ) ( NYSE: LAR ) today announced its second quarter 2026 results. Unless otherwise stated, results are presented in United States dollars on a 100% basis. Sam Pigott, Lithium Argentina’s CEO , commented: "Cauchari-Olaroz delivered another quarter of consistent, strong performance, generating more than $141 million of free cash flow from operations. The team safely completed a planned shutdown while advancing optimization and debottlenecking initiatives and remaining on track to achieve production guidance. "This cash generation enabled a $114 million reduction in net debt while supporting distributions to the joint venture partners. The operation further strengthened its balance sheet, entering new debt facilities with international banks at an attractive interest rate under 5%, providing added flexibility to support future distributions and fund growth plans. "As we look ahead, we continue to take a disciplined approach to growth. Together with Ganfeng, we have agreed to a modular approach to Stage 2 that we believe can accelerate the initial 10,000 tpa of growth capacity, leveraging our partner's expertise in the procurement of advanced processing equipment for installation at site. With RIGI approval now in place, early development activities are underway and we look forward to sharing an updated development plan in the coming months. "With high-quality, low-cost operations, meaningful cash flow generation and a clear, phased path to growth, we believe the Company is well positioned to deliver long-term value for our shareholders." Highlights Cauchari-Olaroz The Company holds a 44.8% equity interest in Exar, the operating entity for Cauchari-Olaroz, and exercises joint control over all key decisions. Operational and financial highlights below are presented on a 100% basis. Production: Produced 9,280 tonnes of lithium carbonate in the second quarter of 2026 with the operation continuing to perform near design capacity. Second quarter production reflected the planned shutdown completed in May 2026 for routine maintenance and plant improvements. The operation averaged 95% of design capacity in the first half of 2026 and remains on track to achieve full-year production guidance of 35,000 - 40,000 tonnes. Operating Costs: Costs of sales for the second quarter of 2026 were $63 million with cash operating costs of $5,897 per tonne1 of lithium carbonate sold. Quarterly costs reflected the planned shutdown, higher energy costs and the impact of a stronger Argentine peso. Pricing: Revenue for the second quarter of 2026 was $174 million, reflecting an average realized price2 of approximately $19,563 per tonne of lithium carbonate sold, representing a cash operating margin2 of 70%. Net Income: Net income for the second quarter of 2026 was $27 million, compared to $49 million for the first quarter of 2026, with the change primarily reflecting a $38 million non-cash deferred tax charge related to accelerated depreciation. Adjusted EBITDA 2 : Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter of 2026 was $110 million, as higher realized prices offset lower sales volumes compared to the first quarter of 2026. Operating Cash Flow: Operating cash flow for the second quarter of 2026 was $142 million and Free Cash Flow from Operations was $141 million3. Liquidity: Cauchari-Olaroz net debt was reduced by $114 million in the second quarter of 2026, after funding $16 million related to cash distributions to Lithium Argentina and Ganfeng. Subsequent to quarter-end, Cauchari-Olaroz completed a $170 million debt facility to reduce financing cost, support additional distributions and provide flexibility to advance the operation's growth plans. Carbon Footprint: Cauchari-Olaroz completed an independent, ISO-verified assessment of its carbon footprint of 1.4 tonnes of CO2e (Scope 1 and 2) per tonne of lithium carbonate produced in 2025. Growth Pipeline Stage 2 Expansion: Continued advancing the expansion plan to increase production capacity by 45,000 tonnes per annum (" tpa ") of LCE at Cauchari-Olaroz (“ Stage 2 ”). RIGI Approval: In May 2026, the Stage 2 expansion was approved under Argentina's Regimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (" RIGI "), providing long-term fiscal stability and enhanced FX and tax benefits. Updated Development Plan: An updated development plan for Stage 2 is expected around the end of the third quarter of 2026 reflecting ongoing engineering and development work. Modular DLE Approach: Together with Ganfeng, the Company is advancing engineering and development of an initial 10,000 tpa LCE modular DLE facility as part of a phased Stage 2 development plan. The strategy is designed to accelerate first production, reduce execution risk and optimize capital efficiency by leveraging Ganfeng's expertise in fabricating advanced process equipment for installation at site. Early Development Activities: Cauchari-Olaroz has approved early development activities for Stage 2, including additional production wells, infrastructure and site preparation, under existing operating permits. These activities are expected to advance the Stage 2 expansion plan and contribute toward investment under RIGI, while strengthening the existing operation and supporting sustained production above current design capacity. Environmental Permitting: The Environmental Impact Assessment (" EIA ") application for Stage 2 has been submitted, with environmental approval process underway. PPG: An integrated development plan targeting capacity of 150,000 tpa of LCE across three phases, leveraging shared infrastructure and the consolidated resource base. Ganfeng and Lithium Argentina continue to advance financing options with potential customers and strategic partners for offtake and minority ownership interests. The RIGI application was submitted in the first quarter of 2026, with approval expected by the end of 2026. Lithium Argentina Financial and Corporate As of June 30, 2026, Lithium Argentina held $100 million in cash and cash equivalents and $230 million in total liquidity, including $130 million undrawn 6-year debt facility. Subsequent to quarter end, Cauchari-Olaroz distributed an additional $27 million to the Company and expects to receive further distributions later in 2026. The Company continued advancing plans for a secondary listing on the Australian Securities Exchange (" ASX "), complementing the Company's NYSE listing and broadening access for Asia-Pacific investors. NON-IFRS AND OTHER FINANCIAL MEASURES Exar Cash Operating Costs and Total Cash Costs per Tonne Lithium Argentina reports Exar’s “ Cash Operating Costs per tonne ” and “ Total Cash Costs per tonne ” as key non-GAAP financial measures or ratios. These non-GAAP financial measures or ratios do not have a standardized meaning under IFRS and might not be comparable to similar financial measures disclosed by other issuers. title: Rocket Lab Successfully Completes 92nd Electron Mission, 8th Launch for iQPS Earth-Imaging Constellation
summary: MAHIA, New Zealand, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, today successfully launched its 13 th Electron rocket of the year to deploy the latest satellite to space for multi-launch customer Institute for Q-shu
body_text: Rocket Lab Successfully Completes 92nd Electron Mission, 8th Launch for iQPS Earth-Imaging Constellation August 6, 2026 PDF Version MAHIA, New Zealand, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, today successfully launched its 13th Electron rocket of the year to deploy the latest satellite to space for multi-launch customer Institute for Q-shu Pioneers of Space, Inc. (iQPS), operators of the QPS-SAR Earth-imaging constellation. ‘The Grain Goddess Provides’ mission launched from Rocket Lab Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand at 9:18 p.m. NZST on August 6, 2026 to deploy the QPS-SAR-13 satellite to space for iQPS that will join its synthetic aperture radar (SAR) constellation providing near-real time imagery across twelve different orbits. This mission was the eighth deployment of a QPS-SAR satellite with 100% mission success by Rocket Lab as Electron continues to serve the iQPS constellation as its primary launch provider. Another 10 dedicated launches are booked on Electron by iQPS to complete their constellation before 2030, showcasing the trust and confidence they have in Rocket Lab’s reliability and performance to deploy the iQPS constellation at scale. ‘The Grain Goddess Provides’ mission was Rocket Lab’s 92nd overall Electron mission. Rocket Lab’s next Electron launch will carry another QPS-SAR satellite on a mission called “The Lightning God Defends”, which is scheduled to take place later this month from LC-1. ‘The Grain Goddess Provides’ launch images: Flight 92 | The Grain Goddess Provides | Flickr ‘The Grain Goddess Provides’ launch broadcast: Rocket Lab - 'The Grain Goddess Provides' Launch - YouTube Rocket Lab Media Contact Murielle Baker media@rocketlabusa.com About Rocket Lab Rocket Lab (Nasdaq: RKLB) is an end-to-end space company delivering rockets, satellites, and spacecraft components for commercial, government, and defense missions. Driven by its industry-leading small-lift rockets Electron and HASTE and its upcoming reusable Neutron medium-lift rocket, Rocket Lab delivers reliable and responsive launch for the world’s most important missions from constellation deployment to missile defense. Rocket Lab’s satellites and components have powered more than 1,700 missions in Earth orbit, as well as deep-space exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Learn more at www.rocketlabcorp.com . title: Announcing the App Portal MCP Server: Debug Webhooks with your Agent
summary: The App Portal now has an MCP server, so your customers can debug the webhooks you send them without ever leaving their editor.
body_text: Svix is the enterprise ready webhooks sending service. With Svix, you can build a secure, reliable, and scalable webhook platform in minutes for both sending and receiving them . Want webhooks in your product without building the hard parts yourself? Give it a try! I'm excited to announce the App Portal MCP server! It lets your customers connect their coding agent to the App Portal , so the agent can debug their integration for them. The agent reads their endpoints, their failed delivery attempts, the payloads you sent them, and the responses their own server gave back instead of them digging through a portal by hand. What the App Portal MCP server is MCP is a standard way to give a coding agent access to something outside itself. A server offers a set of tools, the agent reads their descriptions, and it decides on its own which ones to call and when. So an MCP server is less an API than a set of capabilities you hand an agent and let it use. Every screen your customers use to debug their webhooks is a tool their agent can call: list the endpoints, check an endpoint's success and failure counts, list the messages you sent, pull up the delivery attempts for one of them, and read the exact status code and response body their server returned. It can also read and edit an endpoint's transformation , resend a single message, and recover an endpoint to replay everything that failed since a given date. And you don't need to host anything because it's a server we operate, and a session is scoped to one application by the token your customer generates, so their agent sees exactly what their portal session sees and nothing else. It shows up as your webhooks Because the App Portal you embed is white-labeled, so is the MCP server. The token carries your brand name, so the server introduces itself to your customer's agent as "Acme Webhooks" and describes itself as "Debug Acme webhook delivery". It also tells the agent when to reach for it: whenever the user mentions Acme, or when the codebase has an Acme webhook handler or Acme signature verification in it. How your customers connect their agent Turn it on in your organization settings , and a "Get MCP Token" button appears in your customers' App Portal. They click it, pick their agent, and paste what it gives them. For Claude Code that's one command: claude mcp add --transport http acme-webhooks "https://mcp.eu.svix.com/app/<app_id>" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_TOKEN>" Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Zed take the same URL and header, and the portal has ready-to-paste config for each. There's no OAuth flow to sit through; the token is the whole setup. Then they just ask. "Why is my invoice.paid endpoint failing?" is enough; nobody has to learn which tool does what. Webhook debugging with your agent Most webhook integration problems are small and legible: a field read from the wrong place, a handler returning a 500 on a payload it didn't expect, an endpoint quietly disabled after too many failures. But hopping to the App Portal to see attempt logs and then going back to the editor to feed your agent the new context is far from the best experience we could provide... And that's where the new App Portal MCP server fits. We're just getting started with MCPs at Svix, and the App Portal server is the first piece. If you're curious where we think the protocol itself is heading, read Fully Event-Driven MCP is Coming . Got any feedback or suggestions? Is anything unclear? Open an issue here ! For more content like this, make sure to follow us on X / Twitter , Mastodon , Github , RSS , or our newsletter for the latest updates for the Svix webhook service , or join the discussion on our community Slack .

title: How to Match RED Multicam Frame Rates for Slow Motion
summary: Learn how to mix RED multicam frame rates, interpret overcranked footage, choose timeline rates, manage proxies, and keep audio sync with native or retimed slow motion.
body_text: The safest rule is simple: pick the timeline frame rate first, then decide which camera angles are meant to stay real-time and which are meant to become native slow motion. Don't start by trying to make every RED clip “match” at import. A 120 fps clip can be correct in more than one way depending on intent, because it can be a real-time 120 fps recording that you may slow down later, or it can be overcranked footage that should immediately play back at 23.976, 25, or 29.97. You need to make that decision before you build the multicam. Multicam relies on duration and sync relationships, and slow motion changes duration. If one angle is playing real-time and another angle is already stretched 5x, those clips are no longer describing the same moment over the same amount of timeline time. The two frame rates that matter on RED RED cameras separate the idea of capture from playback. The recording frame rate , sometimes called the capture frame rate or sensor frame rate, is how many frames the camera records per second. The project time base is the rate at which that footage is intended to play back. If the recording frame rate is higher than the project time base, the camera is overcranking and the clip plays as slow motion. If the recording frame rate is lower than the project time base, it plays as fast motion. So a clip recorded at 96 fps with a 24 fps project time base is usually a 24 fps clip containing 96 captured frames per second of action, played back at one quarter speed. That's native slow motion. The important RED-side settings are: Project time base: the intended playback rate, often 23.976 for cinema-style work, 25 for PAL regions, or 29.97 for NTSC/broadcast-style work. Recording frame rate: the capture rate, such as 48, 60, 96, 120, or higher depending on the camera, sensor format, REDCODE, and other settings. Sensor format and resolution: these affect the maximum frame rate available. REDCODE compression: crews often use higher compression ratios when a higher frame rate is required or storage is limited. Audio and recording mode: off-speed and special recording modes can affect whether usable production audio is captured. The mistake is treating “120 fps” as the edit rate. For the edit, the useful question is: should this clip occupy real time or slow-motion time? The same high-frame-rate clip can occupy normal event time or expand into slow-motion time. Choose the timeline rate, not the fastest camera rate In most jobs, set the multicam timeline to the delivery or edit base rate, not the highest capture rate on set. If the show is 23.976, build the timeline at 23.976. If the show is 25, build it at 25. If the broadcast deliverable is 29.97, build there unless post has a specific reason to cut elsewhere. This keeps titles, turnovers, timecode references, exports, review files, and audio workflows predictable. It also keeps the assistant editor from having to explain why the timeline is 59.94 when the whole show is being finished at 23.976. A typical RED multicam slow-motion setup might look like this: A camera: 23.976 project time base, 23.976 recording frame rate, normal sync sound. B camera: 23.976 project time base, 48 recording frame rate, 50 percent slow motion. C camera: 23.976 project time base, 96 recording frame rate, 25 percent slow motion. Multicam for dialogue or continuous performance: real-time angles only, unless your team retimes the slow cameras back to real-time for sync. Slow-motion selects: use overcranked angles as inserts, cutaways, or dedicated slow-motion sections. That last distinction matters because a 96 fps angle playing at 23.976 isn't a normal synced multicam angle for a two-minute performance. It's a slow-motion version of that performance and will run roughly four times longer than the real-time cameras. Native slow motion versus retimed slow motion There are two common ways slow motion enters the edit, and they behave differently. The camera creates native slow motion because the RED records more frames than the project time base, and the file metadata tells the NLE to play those frames at the project rate. Motion is smooth because every playback frame comes from a real captured frame, up to the limits of the chosen speed. A 96 fps recording played at 23.976 gives you about 25 percent speed. A 48 fps recording played at 23.976 gives you about 50 percent speed. You create retimed slow motion in the NLE. A clip that plays real-time in the edit is slowed down after the fact. If there are enough source frames, the NLE can use those real frames. If not, it has to repeat frames, blend frames, or synthesize motion using optical flow or another interpolation method. For RED multicam, the cleanest workflow is to label the intent early: Real-time coverage: keep duration matched to actual event time. Native slow-motion coverage: allow the clip to play longer than real time using the RED project time base. Flexible high-frame-rate coverage: keep it real-time for sync, then slow down selected edits later. Problem footage: clips where the camera project time base doesn't match the intended final time base. The practical consequence is straightforward: native slow-motion clips are great for beauty shots, action details, sports, music-video inserts, product shots, and emotional cutaways. They aren't automatically great as synced multicam angles for continuous live action unless you first convert them to real-time speed for the multicam. Building a multicam when angles have different frame rates A multicam clip wants all angles to represent the same clock time. If camera A records a clap at 01:00:00:00 and the subject walks across frame for ten seconds, every real-time angle should cover that same ten seconds. If camera B is already playing native slow motion, that same walk might last forty seconds in the browser. Syncing those two as if they're equivalent will create confusion immediately. There are three practical patterns that work. Multicam pattern Best use case How to treat high-frame-rate RED clips Main risk Real-time multicam with slow motion later Continuous sync work such as concerts, interviews, unscripted scenes, live events, and sports coverage Convert or retime overcranked clips to real-time duration before building the multicam, then slow selected shots later If a native slow-motion clip stays slow inside the multicam, it will not match the real-time angles Normal-speed multicam plus separate slow-motion selects Scenes where the editor needs reliable angle switching, but also wants beauty shots, inserts, or cutaways Keep real-time cameras in the multicam and organize overcranked clips separately at native slow-motion playback Slow-motion material may be harder to find if bins and naming do not clearly label intent Dedicated slow-motion multicam Multiple cameras intentionally covering the same action at the same slow-motion playback relationship Use angles with matching overcrank relationships, or manually retime them so the same action has matching duration Mixing 48 fps and 96 fps slow-motion angles without adjustment makes the same action run for different lengths The first pattern is a real-time multicam with optional slow motion later. Use all angles at real-time duration. For high-frame-rate RED clips that import as native slow motion, speed them up to match real-time before building the multicam. For example, a 96-over-23.976 clip needs to run at about 400 percent to match real time. Cut the multicam normally, then apply slow motion to selected edits after flattening, committing, or otherwise separating the chosen angle from the multicam structure. This is the best pattern for concerts, interviews, unscripted scenes, live events, sports coverage with continuous sync, and anything where the editor needs normal angle switching. The second pattern is a normal-speed multicam plus separate slow-motion selects. Build the multicam from synced real-time cameras only. Keep overcranked RED clips in a separate bin or stringout at their native slow-motion playback. The editor cuts the multicam for the scene, then uses slow-motion clips as inserts where sync continuity is less important. This is often the cleanest assistant-editor workflow because it avoids forcing slow-motion material into a structure that doesn't need it. The third pattern is a dedicated slow-motion multicam. This only works cleanly when you intend the relevant cameras to play back at the same slow-motion rate, or when you manually conform them into matching slow-motion durations. For example, two RED cameras both recording 96 fps against a 23.976 project time base can form a useful slow-motion multicam because they share the same playback relationship. But mixing one 48 fps slow angle and one 96 fps slow angle in the same slow-motion multicam means the same action will play at different durations unless you retime one of them. The takeaway: multicam sync is about shared time. Slow motion deliberately changes time, so decide which side wins for each group of clips. Multicam sync depends on shared real time; native slow motion changes the clip’s duration. Interpreting RED footage correctly in the NLE Most major NLEs can work with R3D files directly, including Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, Final Cut Pro, and Avid workflows depending on the exact setup. The frame-rate metadata usually comes through, but assistants still need to inspect clips rather than assuming the bin column tells the whole story. For RED media, look for both the capture/recording rate and the playback/project rate. A clip may have been captured at 120 fps but play back at 23.976. In the edit, that clip behaves like a 23.976 slow-motion clip, not like a 120 fps sequence. In Premiere Pro, import RED camera cards through the Media Browser rather than dragging individual file chunks from the filesystem. R3D clips can be split into 4 GB portions during recording, and proper card-level import helps the application index them as unified clips. In Resolve, set project and Camera RAW preferences before bringing in large batches when possible, then confirm how Resolve decodes and interprets the RED clips. Resolve is commonly used for R3D workflows and gives you strong access to RED RAW settings, but timeline frame rate decisions can become harder to change once the project is underway. In Final Cut Pro, RED RAW settings applied to original R3D clips can update reference clips such as synced clips, compound clips, and multicam clips. That's useful, but it also means your team should be deliberate about when they adjust RAW settings versus when they create editorial structures. Avoid creating unnecessary optimized or proxy media at import if the workflow depends on later RAW adjustments. Across NLEs, the practical inspection points are: Does the clip duration match real time or slow-motion time? Does the playback frame rate match the show timeline? Does the metadata show a higher recording frame rate than project time base? Does the clip include usable audio? Are proxies, transcodes, and camera originals using the same starting timecode? Are high-frame-rate clips labeled by intent, not just by fps? If a 120 fps clip is supposed to be slow and it plays in real time, conform or interpret it to the timeline rate. If a 120 fps clip is supposed to sync with real-time cameras and it plays slow, apply a speed change for the multicam version. Keeping audio sync when frame rates differ Audio is where frame-rate mistakes become expensive. Picture can look “close enough” for a while, but audio drift exposes a bad interpretation quickly. Start with this assumption: production sync sound belongs to real-time recording, not to overcranked slow motion. RED support guidance for missing audio points directly at varispeed and special recording modes as things to disable when your team expects audio. In other words, if the sensor frame rate differs from the project time base, don't assume the camera audio will be present or useful, so confirm it. Stable sync audio belongs with real-time footage, while slow-motion picture is cut visually against it. For dialogue, performance, and event coverage, use a stable real-time audio source: External recorder running at the production sample rate. Camera audio from a real-time camera. Timecode sync or jammed timecode across cameras and audio devices. Slate or waveform sync as a fallback. Clear notes identifying which RED angles are off-speed. When you use the high-frame-rate RED angle as native slow motion, its audio usually shouldn't drive sync. Use the real-time audio bed and cut the slow-motion picture against it creatively. If you need a slow-motion shot to line up with a specific beat, clap, impact, or lyric, align the visual event to the real-time audio in the timeline. Don't try to make the whole slow-motion clip maintain sync over its full duration. Be careful with frame-rate override tools. REDCINE-X PRO has frame-rate override features, but changing the frame rate can remove audio from the clip. That isn't a small side effect if your editorial team relies on scratch tracks or embedded camera audio. If you need to change playback interpretation, preserve the original media and keep any audio sync work traceable. A particularly dangerous case is footage recorded with the wrong project time base . For example, if a camera recorded something with a 23.98 project time base but the final needs to be 29.97, a direct export that simply changes the rate can speed up both picture and audio and create sync problems. Your team needs proper standards conversion for that kind of conversion, not a casual reinterpret. Handling mixed 23.976, 25, 29.97, 50, 59.94, and 120 Mixed-rate jobs are common now: RED A-cam at 23.976, drone at 59.94, action camera at 119.88, broadcast source at 29.97, archive at 25. The decision tree is still the same, but you need to separate “different acquisition standard” from “intentional slow motion.” There are a few common cases: 47.952 or 48 captured for 23.976 or 24 playback: usually half-speed native slow motion. 59.94 captured for 23.976 playback: often 40 percent speed if you conform it, or real-time with frame sampling if you leave it as normal 59.94. 50 captured for 25 playback: usually half-speed native slow motion. 119.88 captured for 23.976 playback: usually 20 percent speed if you conform it. 29.97 source in a 23.976 show: usually a standards/conversion issue, not automatically slow motion. 25 source in a 23.976 show: usually a standards/conversion and audio pitch/sync issue, not automatically slow motion. Don't conform everything to the timeline rate just because the timeline is 23.976. Conforming changes duration, which is exactly what you want for native slow motion, and exactly what you don't want for normal-speed documentary, broadcast, or archive sources. For non-RED sources, variable frame rate can also cause trouble, especially with phones, screen recordings, and some action cameras. RED R3D isn't usually the source of variable-frame-rate weirdness, but a multicam project may contain those files alongside RED. Normalize those sources before relying on waveform or timecode sync. Proxies and transcodes need the same timing story Proxy workflow can hide frame-rate problems until conform. If the proxy is interpreted one way and the R3D original is interpreted another way, the edit may relink with different durations, different start frames, or different timecode behavior. Proxy and original media need matching timing so relink doesn't reveal drift or mismatched duration. For RED multicam slow motion, your proxy specs should carry the same timing as the source used for cutting. If the native R3D plays as 23.976 slow motion, the proxy should also play as 23.976 slow motion with matching duration and timecode. If you create a real-time version of a high-frame-rate clip for multicam sync, name and track it as a derived real-time version so nobody mistakes it for the native slow-motion source. Keep these versions clearly separated: Camera original R3D. Native slow-motion proxy or transcode. Real-time retimed proxy or transcode for multicam. Flattened or committed retimes. Color turnover media or XML/AAF references. R3D workflows also use metadata and sidecar files for non-destructive adjustments. That's a strength of the format, but it means your team needs to know whether a change lives in metadata, a proxy, a rendered transcode, an NLE speed effect, or a source interpretation override. Failure modes that show up in the edit Most frame-rate problems are visible if you know what to look for. They usually show up before finishing, but only if your assistants test the actual multicam workflow instead of only checking that files import. Common failure modes include: A high-frame-rate angle drifts out of sync because it's playing native slow motion inside a real-time multicam. A slow-motion clip plays real-time because the NLE interpreted the capture frame rate instead of the intended playback rate. A clip becomes longer after relink because the proxy and R3D were conformed differently. Embedded camera audio disappears after a frame-rate override. A 23.976 to 29.97 conversion speeds up picture and audio instead of doing a proper frame-rate conversion. Document intent and make the NLE match that intent. A practical handoff note for the post team For every RED roll or camera card, your editorial team should be able to answer four questions: what was the project time base, what was the recording frame rate, should the clip play real-time or slow, and where does sync audio come from? That can be as simple as bin columns and clip naming. For example: A001_CamA_23.976_RT B014_CamB_96over23.976_NATIVE_SLOMO C022_CamC_120_REALTIME_FOR_MULTICAM D003_59.94_SOURCE_CONVERT_TO_23.976 The shared understanding matters more than the exact naming style. Editors shouldn't have to guess whether a 120 fps shot is supposed to be a slow-motion insert or a normal-speed angle with extra frames available for later. The right RED multicam frame-rate workflow is a set of deliberate choices: timeline rate based on delivery, RED playback based on project time base, multicam sync based on real-time duration, and slow motion applied only where it belongs. Once those choices are explicit, mixed RED frame rates become manageable instead of mysterious. FAQ Usually no. Set the timeline to the editorial or delivery frame rate, such as 23.976, 25, or 29.97. A 120 fps RED clip is normally a high capture rate, not the edit rate. Decide whether that clip should play as native slow motion or be retimed to real-time before adding it to a multicam. A native slow-motion clip has a longer playback duration than the real-time event it recorded. For example, 96 fps captured for 23.976 playback runs about four times longer than real time. If you place that angle in a real-time multicam without retiming it, it may line up at the slate but drift immediately because it's no longer representing the same clock time as the other cameras. Recording frame rate is how many frames the camera captures per second. Project time base is the rate at which those frames are intended to play back. If a RED camera records 96 fps with a 23.976 project time base, the clip is intended to play back as smooth slow motion at roughly 25 percent speed. Don't assume it will be available or usable. Off-speed and varispeed recording can affect embedded camera audio, and some modes may not record audio as expected. For sync sound, use an external recorder, a real-time camera angle, timecode sync, or a slate and waveform reference. Treat overcranked picture as a visual source unless production confirms otherwise. Proxies should match the timing intent of the source used in editorial. If the R3D plays as native 23.976 slow motion, the proxy should have the same slow-motion duration and timecode relationship. If you make a separate real-time version for multicam sync, label it clearly as a derived retimed version so it isn't confused with the native slow-motion source. Don't rely on fps alone. Use naming, bin columns, and shared metadata fields for intent, such as native slow motion, real-time for multicam, or standards conversion needed. Aspect can help teams carry those intent labels with custom metadata so assistants, editors, and post supervisors are reading the same timing story.

title: Surgeon Removed from Medical Register After Serious Surgical Error Put Patient's Life at Risk

body_text: Medical professionals are entrusted with carrying out life-saving procedures with precision, care, and accountability. However, when serious mistakes occur in the operating room, the consequences can be devastating for patients and their families. A recent decision by the UK Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service (MPTS) has drawn significant attention after an NHS locum surgeon was permanently removed from the medical register following a catastrophic surgical error that experts described as one of the worst they had ever encountered. The case has sparked discussions about patient safety, surgical oversight, professional accountability, and the importance of maintaining high clinical standards across healthcare systems. A Surgical Procedure That Went Terribly Wrong Dr. Yasser Adly Abdel Rahman, an Egyptian-trained surgeon who was working as an NHS locum, performed an emergency bowel operation on a young patient at Royal Oldham Hospital on 25 August 2020. According to evidence presented during the tribunal hearing, the surgery was carried out incorrectly, resulting in a highly unusual and dangerous reconstruction of the patient's digestive system. Instead of restoring the bowel correctly, the procedure connected the organs in a way that created a closed loop. This caused bowel contents leaving the stomach to circulate back into the stomach rather than continuing through the digestive tract. Medical experts stated that this type of reconstruction is not recognized in modern surgical practice and posed an immediate threat to the patient's survival. Patient Endured Severe Pain Following the operation, the patient experienced intense and uncontrollable pain. Despite clear signs that something had gone wrong, the tribunal heard that Dr. Rahman failed to acknowledge the possibility of a surgical mistake. Concerns were reportedly raised by: The patient's parents Hospital medical staff Other healthcare professionals involved in the patient's care Even with these warnings, the surgeon allegedly did not investigate whether complications from the surgery were responsible for the patient's deteriorating condition. Fortunately, another surgeon later performed emergency corrective surgery, preventing what experts believed could have been a fatal outcome. Expert Witness Delivers Damning Assessment One of the most striking moments during the hearing came from an experienced consultant general and colorectal surgeon acting as an expert witness for the General Medical Council (GMC). The expert described the operation as something that was "not known to man," highlighting how unusual and medically unacceptable the procedure was. The tribunal also heard that the mistakes made during surgery were among the most severe surgical errors imaginable. Such testimony played a significant role in demonstrating the seriousness of the misconduct and its potential consequences for patient safety. Tribunal Finds Serious Professional Misconduct The Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service reviewed both the surgical errors and Dr. Rahman's conduct after the operation. The panel concluded that: The surgical procedure fell well below accepted medical standards. The surgeon failed to recognize or properly respond to postoperative complications. The patient was exposed to unnecessary suffering and significant risk. Confidence in the medical profession would be undermined if such conduct were not addressed appropriately. Ultimately, the tribunal ruled that the misconduct was fundamentally incompatible with continued medical registration. As a result, Dr. Rahman was erased from the UK medical register, meaning he is no longer permitted to practise medicine in the United Kingdom. Previous Restrictions Were Ignored The case also involved concerns unrelated to the operation itself. Following the initial investigation, restrictions were placed on Dr. Rahman's ability to practise medicine in July 2021. However, tribunal documents stated that he later secured employment as a locum doctor at Affidea Express Care Clinic in Ireland in February 2022 despite those restrictions. The panel considered this a serious breach of professional obligations and viewed it as an aggravating factor when determining the final sanction. Ignoring regulatory restrictions can significantly affect disciplinary decisions because it raises further concerns about a doctor's willingness to comply with professional standards. Doctor Denied Responsibility Dr. Rahman did not attend the tribunal hearing and was not represented by legal counsel. Instead, he maintained that he had become the victim of unfair treatment. According to tribunal records, he claimed he had been made a "scapegoat" following the operation and described the investigation as a "witch hunt." Despite these assertions, the tribunal found sufficient evidence to support the allegations of misconduct. The panel determined that the seriousness of both the surgical errors and the subsequent professional conduct justified permanent removal from the medical register. Why This Case Matters Cases involving surgical negligence are relatively uncommon, but they receive considerable public attention because they directly affect trust in healthcare systems. Patients undergoing emergency surgery are often in vulnerable situations where they rely entirely on medical teams to deliver safe and effective treatment. Professional regulatory bodies such as the General Medical Council and the Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service exist to ensure that doctors maintain appropriate standards of competence, ethics, and patient care. When those standards are not met, disciplinary action helps protect future patients while maintaining public confidence in the profession. The Importance of Accountability in Healthcare Healthcare professionals work in high-pressure environments where complications can occur despite appropriate treatment. However, regulators distinguish between unavoidable medical complications and conduct that falls significantly below accepted professional standards. Accountability involves more than technical skill. It also requires: Recognizing complications promptly Responding appropriately to patient deterioration Communicating honestly with colleagues and families Following professional regulatory requirements Cooperating with investigations Maintaining these standards helps ensure safer outcomes for patients while reinforcing public trust in healthcare providers. Lessons for Medical Professionals This tribunal highlights several important lessons for surgeons and healthcare organizations. Continuous training, peer review, adherence to clinical guidelines, and effective postoperative monitoring all play critical roles in reducing preventable harm. Equally important is a willingness to acknowledge when complications arise and to seek assistance quickly if concerns are raised. Early intervention can often prevent serious outcomes and improve patient recovery. Conclusion The removal of Dr. Yasser Adly Abdel Rahman from the UK medical register represents one of the most serious disciplinary outcomes available to medical regulators. The tribunal concluded that the combination of severe surgical errors, failure to recognize postoperative complications, and breaches of professional restrictions made continued registration incompatible with patient safety. While most medical procedures are performed successfully every day by highly skilled healthcare professionals, this case serves as a reminder of the importance of clinical competence, transparency, accountability, and robust regulatory oversight in protecting patients. Disclaimer This article is intended for informational and educational purposes only. It summarizes publicly reported information regarding a medical regulatory tribunal and should not be interpreted as legal or medical advice. The findings discussed reflect the conclusions of the Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service based on evidence presented during its proceedings. Source BBC News, Published 4 August 2026.

title: Launching External Web Access for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Launching External Web Access for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock
body_text: Earlier this month, we announced Web Search on Amazon Bedrock , a built-in server-side tool that allows you to ground model responses with current web knowledge, while maintaining data within your secured AWS environment with zero data egress. Today, we are expanding Web Search to enable the external_web_access parameter allowing Web Search to retrieve content directly from the public web so models can ground responses in the latest information. To enable external_web_access, grant the bedrock-websearch:ExternalWebAccess IAM permission to the request identity and leave the external_web_access parameter at its default of true. In doing so, Web Search can then fetch content live from the public web for use cases that need the freshest possible information, such as latest sports score, live pricing, or newly released documentation. If handling sensitive data, to keep retrieval entirely within your AWS boundary, set external_web_access: false. By setting it false, Web Search serves results only from Amazon's in-AWS web index and knowledge graph, with no request data leaving the AWS boundary. Enabling External Web Access is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). To learn more, read our blog post Introducing Web Search on Amazon Bedrock for foundation model grounding, review Controlling external web access in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for cost details.

title: App Featuring AI Smart Search and Industry-First Working Code Promise
summary: As RetailMeNot celebrates its 20th anniversary, the company today announced the launch of the RetailMeNot Rewards app, marking the largest product transformation in its history and introducing a new vision for the future of shopping.
body_text: The new app combines RetailMeNot Rewards loyalty perks, proprietary Scout Price™ technology and conversational AI Smart Search. The RetailMeNot Rewards app is available now on iOS and Android. AUSTIN, Texas, Aug. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As RetailMeNot celebrates its 20th anniversary, the company today announced the launch of the RetailMeNot Rewards app, marking the largest product transformation in its history and introducing a new vision for the future of shopping. RetailMeNot Rewards Logo For two decades, RetailMeNot has helped millions of consumers save money through trusted coupons, promo codes and cash back. As AI reshapes product discovery, RetailMeNot is evolving beyond its origins as a savings destination into an intelligent, personalized shopping platform. This evolution reflects shifting consumer habits: proprietary RetailMeNot research reveals that only 7% of shoppers make purchases without prior research, 59% regularly compare prices and over half already use AI-powered tools to guide buying decisions. Rather than toggling across multiple platforms, consumers increasingly demand a single destination for verified savings and AI discovery—combining trusted savings, loyalty and personalization into one experience built for shoppers, not algorithms. "RetailMeNot has always been about helping people save, but the way consumers shop has fundamentally changed," said Magali Darling, Chief Commercial Officer at RetailMeNot. "As we celebrate 20 years, we're creating an experience shoppers genuinely want to return to. The RetailMeNot Rewards app gives consumers confidence that they'll get verified savings while making every shopping trip more personalized. At the same time, we're creating stronger, more meaningful connections between retailers and high-intent shoppers to drive loyalty beyond one-time transactions." The RetailMeNot Rewards app introduces several key innovations designed to simplify modern shopping: Working Code Promise. Exclusive to the RetailMeNot app, the Working Code Promise solves an industry-wide problem in a unique way by verifying every promo code for participating merchants before it's presented to shoppers. By eliminating the "checkout letdown" caused by expired or invalid codes, the app delivers a more trusted and seamless savings experience, giving shoppers greater confidence that the savings they see are the savings they'll get. Guaranteed Savings. Establishes guaranteed minimum 1% cash back across more than 3,500 participating merchants in the app. Guaranteed cash back can be stacked with eligible promo codes and other offers for predictable, transparent savings. RetailMeNot Rewards. An app-exclusive loyalty program where members earn $5 for every two qualifying purchases of $25 or more each month at eligible merchants. Members can earn up to $50 in bonus rewards each month, giving shoppers even more reasons to return while helping retailers build stronger customer loyalty. Scout Price™ (Beta). RetailMeNot's proprietary pricing technology helps shoppers find the best available price on products by automatically factoring in applicable cash back offers and other eligible savings. By doing the math for you, Scout Price makes it easier to shop with confidence and maximize your savings. Currently in beta, Scout Price will continue expanding in coming weeks to support exclusive codes, additional retailers and product offers. Personalized Shopping. Customized offers, curated product recommendations and shopping feeds tailored to each member's interests and purchasing behavior make it easier to discover relevant deals. Smart Search. A conversational AI shopping feature that allows consumers to discover products, compare brands and find active deals using natural language search queries.

title: What Not To Do When Deploying Dealership AI
summary: Common pitfalls dealerships hit when rolling out AI, and how to avoid them.
body_text: ← Blog What Not To Do When Deploying Dealership AI Common pitfalls dealerships hit when rolling out AI, and how to avoid them. By Chris · August 2025 In 2022, Klarna decided to replace 700 customer service jobs with AI tools. While seeking speed and cost savings, the company faced reduced customer satisfaction and public backlash, demonstrating that rapid AI implementation without proper planning can backfire. The pitfalls of poor AI implementation Klarna's rushed adoption overlooked critical factors: setting realistic expectations, transparent communication with employees and customers, and maintaining human oversight for nuanced interactions. This approach resulted in quality concerns and diminished trust. What dealerships can learn from Klarna's mistakes 1. Speed thoughtfully AI should enhance your operations, not overhaul them overnight. Start with a single workflow like scheduling, measure impact, then expand to prevent frustration and resistance. 2. Adopt a clear approach AI implementation mistakes often stem from attempting full task replacement. Instead, AI should handle repetitive, low-stakes work, freeing staff for high-value interactions. 3. Set clear expectations Customers prefer transparent, competent assistance. Train systems to acknowledge AI limitations and escalate complex issues to humans. What Toma does differently Toma positions itself around authentic, realistic AI deployment rather than overpromising. Toma's AI can handle routine scheduling 24/7, route and filter calls appropriately, automate appointment confirmations and reminders, and automate roughly 75% of inbound calls. It can't yet deliver repair status updates, handle complex complaints, or replace high-touch, contextual conversations. ROI stems from getting it right Returns come from productivity gains and revenue protection, not headcount reduction. Proper implementation eliminates missed calls, unattended customers, and no-shows. Early-stage automotive AI adoption rewards thoughtful, customer-focused dealers who understand realistic implementation.

title: How to Check Your Prepaid Meter Balance in Nigeria
summary: Have you ever been in the middle of watching your favourite TV show, working from home, or preparing dinner when your electricity suddenly goes off? You rush to your prepaid meter only to discover you've run out of electricity units. It's a situation many Nigerians can relate to. The good
body_text: Have you ever been in the middle of watching your favourite TV show, working from home, or preparing dinner when your electricity suddenly goes off? You rush to your prepaid meter only to discover you've run out of electricity units. It's a situation many Nigerians can relate to. The good news is that checking your prepaid meter balance is quick and easy. By monitoring your remaining units regularly, you can plan your next recharge and avoid unexpected blackouts. What Is a Prepaid Meter Balance? Your prepaid meter balance is the number of electricity units (measured in kilowatt-hours or kWh) remaining on your meter. Every time you use electricity, your meter deducts units based on your energy consumption. Once your balance reaches zero, your electricity supply will automatically disconnect until you purchase and load another token. Why You Should Check Your Meter Balance Regularly Many people only check their meter after the lights go off. Instead, make it a habit to monitor your balance every few days. Regular checks help you: Avoid Unexpected Power Interruptions You'll know when it's time to recharge before your units run out. Manage Your Monthly Budget Tracking your usage helps you estimate how much electricity you consume each month. Detect High Energy Consumption If your units finish faster than usual, it could indicate increased electricity usage or inefficient appliances. Ways to Check Your Prepaid Meter Balance The exact method depends on your meter manufacturer. Here are the most common ways. Method 1: Check Using Your Meter Keypad Most prepaid meters have a keypad that allows you to check your remaining balance. Simply: Wake up the meter if the screen is blank. Enter the balance code recommended for your meter. Press the Enter or OK button. Your remaining units should appear on the screen. Note: Meter codes differ by manufacturer. Always refer to your meter's user manual or contact your electricity distribution company (DisCo) if you're unsure of the correct code. Method 2: Check the Meter Display Some modern prepaid meters automatically display important information in rotation, including: Remaining units Meter number Current consumption Voltage Load information Simply wait a few seconds for the display to cycle through the available information. Method 3: Use Your DisCo's Customer Portal Some electricity distribution companies provide online portals where customers can: Check account information View payment history Monitor electricity consumption Access customer support Availability depends on your DisCo and meter type. Method 4: Check Through Your Smart Meter App If you're using a smart prepaid meter, you may be able to monitor your electricity usage through the manufacturer's mobile application. Depending on your meter, the app may display: Real-time balance Daily usage Monthly consumption Recharge history Common Prepaid Meter Brands in Nigeria Nigeria has several prepaid meter manufacturers. Some common brands include: Hexing Mojec Conlog Longi Holley EDMI Although the process is generally similar, the specific balance codes may vary. What to Do If Your Meter Isn't Displaying Your Balance Sometimes your meter may fail to display your remaining units. Possible reasons include: Low Battery (for CIU Units) Some Customer Interface Units (CIUs) use batteries. Replace the batteries if the screen won't turn on. Faulty Display If the screen is damaged or blank, contact your DisCo immediately. Meter Communication Issues Some split prepaid meters may temporarily lose communication between the interface unit and the meter. Restart the interface unit and try again. Meter Fault If the issue persists, report it to your electricity distribution company for inspection.
